rule: top-level `file.fun` (file basename); nested modules/functors dotted (`file.Make.connect`); local function lets `outer.f`, local value lets fold into the enclosing binding; module-level code's caller is the module. Names resolve in definition order through local bindings, local opens, enclosing structures and their opens/includes, module aliases (`module F = Filegen.Make (P)`) and dune library wrappers (`Functoria.DSL`); then Stdlib (`Stdlib.invalid_arg`), the innermost external local open, the one external open (medium); `List.length` medium; applying a parameter is unknown. Top-level / file-level code (outside any function or type): the caller is the file's module ID. Languages with a module qualifier use it (Python module, JS/TS module, Lua module, OCaml/Haskell module, Rust module path `crate::a::b`, Groovy `pkg.Script#run`). Each call in a multi-line method chain is reported on the line of its own method name, not the chain's first line.
notes: Top-level functions are `file.fun` with the file basename `calc`. Bare Stdlib values are `Stdlib.<name>`, medium (OCaml note: then Stdlib (`Stdlib.invalid_arg`)); qualified Stdlib submodule calls are named as written, medium (`List.length` medium). `let () = ...` is module-level code: caller is the module `calc`. In `report`, each callee of the multi-line application is on its own name's line (`String.concat` line 7, `List.map` line 9, `List.rev` line 11); `describe` on line 10 is passed, not applied: no edge. List literals are data construction.
